_readme: SEED FILE. `scripts/seed.ts` is the only code path that opens this
directory, and nothing here is read at runtime: Postgres is the
single source of truth once a row lands, so an edit below changes
nothing until the next seed pass applies it.
Keys beginning with an underscore are stripped by the loader before
anything is validated or written, which is what lets a seed file
carry this header at all. A seed is usually met on its own, in a
diff or an editor tab, where nothing about the content says which
path owns it.
This file seeds `categories`. A category is upserted by the
(domain, key) pair `categories_domain_id_key_unique` holds, so a
second seed pass rewrites the same row rather than adding a rival
one that a term or a `criteria` row would then have to choose
between.
`domainSlug` is not a column. `categories.domain_id` holds a key
the database issues, and no seed file can know one before the
domain row is written, so a category names its domain by the only
key an author owns: the slug `domains.json` seeds. The loader
resolves it, and refuses a category naming a slug the bundle does
not carry.
`parentKey` is the same substitution one level down, standing in
for `categories.parent_id`, and every row below carries it as null.
Null is written out rather than left off because a root is not a
category missing a parent: it is the ordinary shape of a flat
taxonomy, and the member is where a child would name the root it
sits under.
Nesting is capped at one level by a trigger on `categories`, which
refuses a parent that is itself a child and a parent belonging to
another domain. Shipping only roots keeps the worked example on the
right side of that cap; a seed test later in this phase asserts it
rather than leaving it to review.
Nothing in the schema fixes this set of three. A `criteria` row
points at a category by foreign key rather than naming one of a
fixed list, so a fourth bucket is a row rather than a migration.
The categories below are illustrative, like the rest of
`example-tech-radar`: they show that a domain sorts its subject
matter into named buckets which terms then hang off, and they stay
neutral about the subject. A real taxonomy belongs to whoever
operates an instance and reaches the database through their own
seeds.
